stem: A developer has a Node.js web app in a local folder. The folder has no `Dockerfile`, and Docker is not installed on the laptop. The developer wants to deploy the app to Cloud Run with the fewest steps. What should the developer do?

options.text: Run `gcloud builds submit --pack image=IMAGE_URL`, and then run `gcloud run deploy SERVICE --image IMAGE_URL`.
Install Docker, build and push the image, and then run `gcloud run deploy SERVICE --image IMAGE_URL`.
Run `gcloud run deploy SERVICE --source .` in the app folder, and answer the prompts.
Add a `cloudbuild.yaml` file, create a Cloud Build trigger, and push the code to a repository.

explanation: `gcloud run deploy --source` builds the image with Cloud Build and Google Cloud's buildpacks, and then deploys it. It needs **no Docker on the laptop and no `Dockerfile`**. It also removes the separate `gcloud builds submit` step, so it has the **fewest steps**.

whyWrong.A: This works without Docker, but it takes two commands. A source deploy builds and deploys with one command.
whyWrong.B: The developer must install Docker and run more steps. A source deploy needs no Docker on the laptop.
whyWrong.D: A build config file and a trigger add setup work. The developer wants the fewest steps for this deploy.

explanation: A source deploy is a convenience feature, and it does not allow full customization of the build. When you need **full control of each build step**, such as tests, scans, and signing **before the deploy**, build the image with Cloud Build. Then deploy the image with `--image`.

stem: A Cloud Run service calls a partner API with a key that is stored in Secret Manager. The app reads the key again before each call. The security team rotates the key every week, and each rotation adds a new secret version. The service must use the new version within minutes, without a new deployment or a new revision. How should you give the secret to the service?

options.text: Mount the secret as a volume, and reference the `latest` version of the secret.
Expose the secret as an environment variable that is pinned to the current version number.
Expose the secret as an environment variable that references the `latest` version.
Copy the key into a plain environment variable with `--update-env-vars` after each rotation.

explanation: When the app reads a secret from a **volume**, Cloud Run fetches the value of the latest version from Secret Manager. This method works well with **secret rotation**, and it needs **no new deployment or revision**.

whyWrong.B: A pinned version never changes. Each new version needs a new deployment, which creates a new revision.
whyWrong.C: Cloud Run resolves an environment variable at instance startup. Running instances keep the old value until they restart.
whyWrong.D: Each change of an environment variable creates a new revision. Google also does not recommend environment variables for secrets.

stem: A Cloud Run service gets a database password from Secret Manager. The password is in an environment variable that references the `latest` version. After a password rotation, logs show that instances of the same revision use different passwords. You want all instances of a revision to use one known value. You also want to control when a new value goes live. What should you do?

options.text: Mount the secret as a volume, and reference the `latest` version.
Disable the old secret version right after each rotation.
Pin the environment variable to a version number, and deploy a new revision for each new version.
Reference the secret with `--set-secrets` instead of `--update-secrets`, and keep the `latest` version.

explanation: Cloud Run resolves a secret in an environment variable **at instance startup**. With `latest`, instances that start after a rotation get the new value, and older instances keep the old one. Google recommends that you **pin a version**. Each revision then has one value, and your next deployment **controls when the new value goes live**.

whyWrong.A: A volume returns the latest version each time the app reads it. The value changes without a deployment, so you cannot control when it goes live.
whyWrong.B: Running instances keep the value that they read at startup. The instances of the revision still use different values.
whyWrong.D: `--set-secrets` replaces the full list of secrets. The variable still resolves `latest` when each instance starts.

stem: You deploy an internal API to Cloud Run. Only other services in your organization call it, and they authenticate with IAM. The API reads data from one Firestore database. Your security team requires least privilege and forbids service account keys. Which two actions should you take when you run `gcloud run deploy`? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set `--service-account` to a user-managed service account with only the Firestore role that it needs.
Set `--allow-unauthenticated`, and check an API key in the application code.
Set `--no-allow-unauthenticated`, so that each caller needs the Cloud Run Invoker role.
Omit `--service-account`, so that the service uses the Compute Engine default service account.
Set `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to the path of a key file that a secret volume provides.

explanation: Google recommends a **user-managed service account** with the minimum permissions as the service identity. This gives the API **least privilege** without keys. `--no-allow-unauthenticated` keeps the service private, so only callers with the Cloud Run Invoker role can call it.

whyWrong.B: This flag grants Cloud Run Invoker to `allUsers` and makes the API public. Callers then do not authenticate with IAM.
whyWrong.D: The Compute Engine default service account is not a minimal identity. Google recommends a user-managed service account.
whyWrong.E: This uses a service account key, which the security team forbids. Never set `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` on a service that uses its service identity.

stem: You write a Python function, `handle_order`. An Eventarc trigger will call it when a file arrives in Cloud Storage. The function must not be public. You want to use the API that Google recommends for Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions). Which command should you run in the source folder?

options.text: `gcloud functions deploy orders-fn --gen2 --runtime python314 --entry-point handle_order --source . --region us-central1`
`gcloud run deploy orders-fn --source . --function handle_order --base-image python314 --region us-central1`
`gcloud run deploy orders-fn --source . --function handle_order --base-image python314 --region us-central1 --allow-unauthenticated`
`gcloud run deploy orders-fn --source . --function handle_order --base-image python314 --region us-central1 --no-invoker-iam-check`

explanation: The **Cloud Run Admin API is the recommended API** for functions, and `gcloud run deploy --function` uses it. An event-triggered function **must not be public**, so you omit `--allow-unauthenticated`.

stem: A Cloud Run service opens its port at once, but it needs about 20 seconds to load data before it can serve requests. The service uses the default TCP startup probe and an HTTP readiness probe on `/ready`. After each scale-out, some requests to the new instances fail. What should you do?

Add a liveness probe that checks the `/ready` endpoint.
Configure an HTTP startup probe on an endpoint that succeeds only after the data is loaded.
Remove the startup probe, so that only the readiness probe controls traffic to new instances.

explanation: Cloud Run **can route traffic to a new instance before the first readiness probe completes**. When the startup probe succeeds, Cloud Run treats the container as ready. Google recommends that **the startup probe also ensures readiness**, so use an HTTP startup probe that passes only after the data loads.

whyWrong.A: A higher threshold makes the readiness probe slower to fail. It does not stop traffic before the first readiness probe completes.
whyWrong.B: A liveness probe finds an instance that is stuck. It does not control when a new instance gets its first requests.
whyWrong.D: If you configure no startup probe, Cloud Run adds a default TCP startup probe. The port opens at once, so the problem stays.

stem: A Deployment with 6 replicas reads `LOG_LEVEL` from a ConfigMap through an environment variable. You changed the value in the ConfigMap an hour ago, but the running Pods still use the old value. The app must stay available while the Pods get the new value. What should you do?

stem: You are designing how to expose a new app on GKE. Requests for `/api` must go to the `api` Service, and all other requests must go to the `web` Service. Both paths must share one external IP address. You want the approach that Google recommends for new designs. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Gateway with the `gke-l7-global-external-managed` GatewayClass, and an HTTPRoute with a path match for `/api`.
Create a LoadBalancer Service with `loadBalancerClass: "networking.gke.io/l4-regional-external"` for each app.
Create an Ingress with path rules for `/api` and `/`, and let GKE create the Application Load Balancer.
Create one LoadBalancer Service that selects the Pods of both apps, and add path rules in a BackendConfig.

explanation: Path routing needs an Application Load Balancer. **GKE Ingress is in maintenance mode**, and Google **recommends the GKE Gateway API**. One Gateway has one IP address, and an HTTPRoute sends `/api` to one Service and other paths to another.

whyWrong.B: A LoadBalancer Service creates a passthrough Network Load Balancer. It cannot route by path, and each Service gets its own IP address.
whyWrong.C: Ingress can route by path, but it is in maintenance mode. Google recommends the Gateway API.
whyWrong.D: A passthrough Network Load Balancer cannot route by path. A BackendConfig does not define routes.

sources.title: GKE Ingress for Application Load Balancers
sources.evidence: GKE Ingress is in maintenance mode. No new functionality will be added except as needed to fix bugs. We recommend that you use GKE Gateway API.

sources.title: About LoadBalancer Services
sources.evidence: External LoadBalancer Services are implemented by using regional external passthrough Network Load Balancers.

stem: A Gateway and an HTTPRoute are in the `frontend` namespace. The HTTPRoute sends `/api` requests to the `api` Service in the `backend` namespace. Requests for `/api` fail. The route status says that the reference to the Service is not permitted. What should you do?

options.text: Create a ReferenceGrant in the `frontend` namespace that allows references to Services in `backend`.
Change the type of the `api` Service in the `backend` namespace from ClusterIP to LoadBalancer.
Create a ReferenceGrant in the `backend` namespace that allows references from HTTPRoutes in `frontend`.
Create a HealthCheckPolicy for the `api` Service in the `backend` namespace.

explanation: A cross-namespace reference needs a **ReferenceGrant in the namespace of the resource being referenced**. The HTTPRoute refers to a Service in `backend`, so the ReferenceGrant goes in `backend`.

whyWrong.A: The ReferenceGrant must be in the namespace of the referenced resource, which is `backend`.
whyWrong.B: The Service type does not allow a cross-namespace reference. The route still needs a ReferenceGrant.
whyWrong.D: A HealthCheckPolicy configures the load balancer health check. It does not allow references from another namespace.

sources.title: About Gateway API
sources.evidence: To enable cross-namespace references, you need a ReferenceGrant in the namespace of the resource being referenced.

sources.title: About Gateway API
sources.evidence: ReferenceGrant acts as a permission provider, specifying which resources (`from`) are allowed to reference other resources (`to`).

stem: You have a VPC-native GKE Standard cluster. The `HttpLoadBalancing` add-on is enabled, but the Gateway API is not. You want to expose an app inside the VPC network with a Gateway that uses the `gke-l7-rilb` GatewayClass. Which two actions must you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Update the cluster with the `--gateway-api=standard` flag.
Create a BackendConfig for each Service that the Gateway routes to.
Create a LoadBalancer Service for each backend before you create the Gateway.
Create a new routes-based cluster, because a Gateway needs routes-based networking.
Create a proxy-only subnet in the region of the cluster.

explanation: On a Standard cluster, `--gateway-api=standard` **installs the Gateway API CRDs**. `gke-l7-rilb` creates an **internal Application Load Balancer**, and a Gateway of this kind needs a **proxy-only subnet** in its region.

whyWrong.B: BackendConfig is an Ingress configuration resource. A Gateway uses Policy resources instead.
whyWrong.C: A Gateway sends traffic to the Services in its HTTPRoutes. It does not need LoadBalancer Services.
whyWrong.D: The Gateway API is supported on VPC-native clusters only.

sources.title: Deploying Gateways
sources.evidence: The `--gateway-api=standard` flag instructs GKE to install the CRDs of the Gateway API Standard Channel with the cluster.

sources.title: Deploying Gateways
sources.evidence: You must configure a proxy-only subnet before you create a Gateway that uses an internal Application Load Balancer.

sources.title: Configure Gateway resources using Policies
sources.evidence: You don't need to create a BackendConfig, because BackendConfig is an Ingress configuration resource.

stem: Pods in a GKE Standard cluster in project `apps-prod` show `ImagePullBackOff`. The image is in an Artifact Registry repository in project `shared-images`. The nodes use the Compute Engine default service account. The Kubernetes ServiceAccount of the Pods already has Artifact Registry Reader on the repository. You must not use service account keys. What should you do?

options.text: Grant Artifact Registry Reader on the repository to the service account of the nodes.
Grant Artifact Registry Reader on the `shared-images` project to the Kubernetes ServiceAccount.
Create an `imagePullSecret` from a service account key, and add it to the Pod spec.
Copy the image to Container Registry in the `apps-prod` project, and change the image path.

explanation: **Nodes pull images as the node service account**, not as the Kubernetes ServiceAccount of the Pod. When the repository is **in a different project**, grant Artifact Registry permissions to the service account that the nodes use.

whyWrong.B: The node pulls the image, not the Pod. A role on the Kubernetes ServiceAccount does not apply to image pulls.
whyWrong.C: This uses a service account key, which the requirement does not allow.
whyWrong.D: Container Registry is shut down, and you cannot write images to it.

sources.title: Deploying to Google Kubernetes Engine
sources.evidence: If GKE is in a different project than Artifact Registry, grant Artifact Registry permissions to the service account that your GKE node use. By default, nodes use the Compute Engine default service account.

sources.title: Deploying to Google Kubernetes Engine
sources.evidence: The Compute Engine default service account is the identity for nodes.

sources.title: Transition from Container Registry
sources.evidence: Effective March 18, 2025, Container Registry is shut down and writing images to Container Registry is unavailable.

stem: An app on a GKE Autopilot cluster must read objects from a Cloud Storage bucket. Other apps in the cluster must not get this access. Your security team forbids service account keys. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable Workload Identity Federation for GKE on the cluster with `gcloud container clusters update`.
Create a Kubernetes ServiceAccount for the app, and set it in `serviceAccountName` in the Pod spec.
Grant a Cloud Storage read role on the bucket to the principal identifier of that Kubernetes ServiceAccount.
Store a service account key in a Kubernetes Secret, and mount the Secret in the Pods of the app.
Grant a Cloud Storage read role on the bucket to the service account of the cluster nodes.

explanation: Workload Identity Federation for GKE is **always enabled in Autopilot**. You grant IAM roles to the **principal identifier of a Kubernetes ServiceAccount**, and only the Pods that use it get the access. This needs **no key files**.

whyWrong.A: Workload Identity Federation for GKE is always enabled in Autopilot. Enabling it also grants no IAM permissions.
whyWrong.D: The security team forbids service account keys. Workload Identity Federation for GKE needs no key files.
whyWrong.E: With Workload Identity Federation for GKE, Pods call Google Cloud APIs as their Kubernetes ServiceAccount, not as the node service account.

sources.title: Authenticate to Google Cloud APIs from GKE workloads
sources.evidence: In Autopilot, Workload Identity Federation for GKE is always enabled.

sources.title: Authenticate to Google Cloud APIs from GKE workloads
sources.evidence: The principal in these policies is an IAM principal identifier that corresponds to the workloads, namespaces, or Kubernetes ServiceAccounts.

sources.title: About Workload Identity Federation for GKE
sources.evidence: Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets you use IAM policies to grant Kubernetes workloads in your GKE cluster access to specific Google Cloud APIs without needing manual configuration or less secure methods like service account key files.

stem: An app on GKE needs a database password. The security team requires that IAM, not in-cluster RBAC, controls access to the password. The password must not be stored in a Kubernetes Secret. What should you do?

options.text: Store the password in a Kubernetes Secret, and turn on application-layer secrets encryption with a Cloud KMS key.
Store the password in a ConfigMap, and limit access to that ConfigMap with namespace RBAC rules.
Store the password in Secret Manager, and use the Secret Manager add-on with the Sync as Kubernetes Secret feature.
Store the password in Secret Manager, mount it with the Secret Manager add-on, and grant access with IAM.

explanation: Secrets outside the cluster let you **control access with IAM instead of in-cluster RBAC rules**. The Secret Manager add-on mounts the password as a file in a CSI volume, so **no Kubernetes Secret** holds it. Grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` to the Kubernetes ServiceAccount of the Pod.

whyWrong.A: Encryption protects the Secret at rest. The password is still in a Kubernetes Secret, and RBAC controls access to it.
whyWrong.B: A ConfigMap gives no secrecy or encryption, and RBAC, not IAM, controls access to it.
whyWrong.C: The Secret Manager add-on does not support the Sync as Kubernetes Secret feature. That feature also stores the password in a Kubernetes Secret.

sources.title: Access secrets stored outside GKE clusters using client libraries
sources.evidence: lets you control access to your secrets using Identity and Access Management (IAM) instead of in-cluster RBAC rules.

sources.title: Use Secret Manager add-on with Google Kubernetes Engine
sources.evidence: The Secret Manager add-on doesn't support the Sync as Kubernetes Secret feature, which is available in the open source Secrets Store CSI Driver.

sources.title: Use Secret Manager add-on with Google Kubernetes Engine
sources.evidence: Pods that use the configured Kubernetes ServiceAccount automatically authenticate as the IAM principal identifier that corresponds to the Kubernetes ServiceAccount when accessing the Secret Manager API.

stem: A team moves a small workload from a GKE Standard cluster to a GKE Autopilot cluster. The CPU request in the Pod spec is less than the minimum that Autopilot allows for the compute class. What happens when the team deploys the workload?

options.text: Autopilot rejects the workload and shows an error message.
Autopilot raises the request to the allowed range, and then runs the Pod.
Autopilot runs the Pod with the CPU request that the Pod spec sets.
Autopilot ignores the request and applies the default requests of the compute class.

explanation: Autopilot validates requests against a **minimum and a maximum** for each compute class. If the requests are **less than the minimum**, Autopilot **modifies the workload configuration** to bring them into the allowed range. The Pod then runs with the larger request.

whyWrong.A: For a request that is less than the minimum, Autopilot raises the request to the allowed range instead.
whyWrong.C: Autopilot enforces the minimum for the compute class. It changes a request that is less than the minimum.
whyWrong.D: Autopilot assigns default requests only to containers that do not specify requests. This container specifies a CPU request.

sources.title: Resource requests in Autopilot
sources.evidence: If your requests are less than the minimum, Autopilot automatically modifies your workload configuration to bring your requests within the allowed range.

sources.title: Resource requests in Autopilot
sources.evidence: If you don't specify requests for some containers, Autopilot assigns default values to let those containers run correctly.

stem: Your team builds a container image in Cloud Build and deploys it to `dev`, `staging`, and `prod` GKE clusters. A deploy to production needs a manual approval. The team must deploy to production the exact image that it tested in `staging`. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Build trigger for each environment that rebuilds the image from the branch and runs `kubectl apply`.
Create a Cloud Deploy pipeline with the three targets, set `requireApproval` on `prod`, and promote one release.
Create a Cloud Deploy pipeline, and create a new release with a new image build for each target.
Deploy the three environments to namespaces in one cluster, and have a reviewer run `kubectl apply` for production.

explanation: Cloud Deploy **promotes one release**, with its exact images, through the targets in order. `requireApproval` on the `prod` target **holds the promotion until someone approves it**. Google recommends that you **build once and promote** the same image.

whyWrong.A: A rebuild for each environment can add untested changes. Google recommends that you build once and promote.
whyWrong.C: A new build for each target deploys an image that was not tested in `staging`.
whyWrong.D: This gives no promotion sequence or approval control. Google also recommends separate clusters for each environment.

sources.title: Overview of Cloud Deploy
sources.evidence: To require approval for a target, set the `requireApproval` property in the target definition.

sources.title: Best practices for continuous integration and delivery to Google Kubernetes Engine
sources.evidence: To ensure that the container image you tested is the container image you deploy, it's best to build once and promote along your environments.

sources.title: Overview of Cloud Deploy
sources.evidence: Cloud Deploy is a managed service that automates delivery of your applications to a series of target environments in a defined promotion sequence.

stem:
An app takes from 1 to 4 minutes to start, depending on the data that it loads. Pods often enter `CrashLoopBackOff` during slow starts. The app has this liveness probe:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
```

After the app starts, the liveness probe must still detect a deadlock in about 15 seconds. What should you do?

options.text: Set `initialDelaySeconds: 240` on the liveness probe, so that it waits for the slowest start.
Set `failureThreshold: 50` on the liveness probe, so that it allows for the slowest start.
Add a startup probe on `/healthz` with `failureThreshold: 30` and `periodSeconds: 10`.
Replace the liveness probe with a readiness probe on the same `/healthz` endpoint.

explanation: A **startup probe** gives the app time to start, and Kubernetes runs the liveness probe **only after the startup probe succeeds**. With 30 × 10 seconds, the app has 5 minutes to start. The **liveness settings stay the same**, so the probe still detects a deadlock in about 15 seconds.

whyWrong.A: The delay applies to every start, also to a fast one. A deadlock soon after a fast start stays undetected until the delay ends.
whyWrong.B: This makes deadlock detection slow for the whole life of the container, about 250 seconds.
whyWrong.D: A readiness failure does not restart the container. A deadlocked container would never restart.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: Rather than set a long liveness interval, you can configure a separate configuration for probing the container as it starts up, allowing a time longer than the liveness interval would allow.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: You should then set its `failureThreshold` high enough to allow the container to start, without changing the default values of the liveness probe. This helps to protect against deadlocks.

stem: A web app on GKE has a liveness probe on `/healthz`. The handler runs a query on the Cloud SQL database and returns HTTP 500 if the query fails. When the database is slow for a few minutes, all Pods restart at the same time, and the outage gets longer. What should you do?

options.text: Increase `timeoutSeconds` on the liveness probe, so that slow queries can complete.
Change `/healthz` to check only the app process, without calls to other services.
Move the database query to a startup probe, and remove the liveness probe.
Replace the HTTP check with an `exec` probe that runs the database query in the container.

explanation: Google says to **never make probe logic access other services**, because slow services can compromise the Pod lifecycle. A liveness probe must show only an **unrecoverable failure**, such as a deadlock. A local check stops the restarts when the database is slow.

whyWrong.A: The probe still depends on the database. A longer slowdown still restarts all Pods.
whyWrong.C: The startup probe still accesses another service. Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes also no longer detects a deadlock.
whyWrong.D: The probe still depends on the database. An `exec` probe also starts new processes each time it runs.

sources.title: Best practices for running cost-optimized Kubernetes applications on GKE
sources.evidence: Never make any probe logic access other services. It can compromise the lifecycle of your Pod if these services don't respond promptly.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: Liveness probes must be configured carefully to ensure that they truly indicate unrecoverable application failure, for example a deadlock.

stem: A service on GKE loads a large cache when it starts. It returns errors until the cache is loaded, which takes about 90 seconds. During each rollout, clients get errors from the new Pods. The app does not deadlock. What should you add?

options.text: A readiness probe that passes only after the cache is fully loaded
A liveness probe that fails until the cache is fully loaded
`initialDelaySeconds: 90` on a new liveness probe for the app
`minReadySeconds: 90` on the Deployment, with no probes added

explanation: Kubernetes sends traffic only to ready Pods. A **readiness probe that passes only after the cache is fully loaded** keeps the new Pods out of the Service endpoints until they can serve.

whyWrong.B: A liveness failure restarts the container. The cache load starts again, and the Pod can restart in a loop.
whyWrong.C: A liveness probe does not control traffic. Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes considers the Pod ready at once.
whyWrong.D: `minReadySeconds` only delays when a ready Pod counts as available. Without a readiness probe, the Pod is ready at once and gets traffic.

sources.title: Best practices for running cost-optimized Kubernetes applications on GKE
sources.evidence: If your application depends on a cache to be loaded at startup, the readiness probe must say it's ready only after the cache is fully loaded.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: If a container does not provide a particular probe, the kubelet always considers the result as `Success`.

stem: You created a GKE Ingress when the Deployment had 0 replicas. Later, you scaled the Deployment up. The Pods have a readiness probe on `/healthz`. The load balancer marks all backends unhealthy, because `/` returns HTTP 404. You cannot recreate the Ingress. What should you do?

options.text: Change `periodSeconds` on the readiness probe, so that GKE copies the probe to the health check again.
Delete the Pods, so that the Ingress controller reads the readiness probe from the new Pods.
Create a HealthCheckPolicy that sets `requestPath: /healthz` for the Service.
Create a BackendConfig with a `healthCheck` that uses `/healthz`, and reference it from the Service.

explanation: The Ingress controller uses the readiness probe **only if the Pods exist when you create the Ingress**. With 0 replicas, the default health check applies, and later probe changes do not affect the Ingress. Google recommends a **BackendConfig** for the most control over the load balancer health check.

whyWrong.A: Changes to the readiness probe do not affect the Ingress after you create it.
whyWrong.B: The controller reads the probe only when you create the Ingress. New Pods do not change the health check.
whyWrong.C: A HealthCheckPolicy configures the health check of a Gateway. An Ingress uses a BackendConfig.

sources.title: GKE Ingress for Application Load Balancers
sources.evidence: For the GKE Ingress controller to use your `readinessProbes` as health checks, the Pods for an Ingress must exist at the time of Ingress creation. If your replicas are scaled to 0, the default health check applies.

sources.title: GKE Ingress for Application Load Balancers
sources.evidence: Changes to a Pod's `readinessProbe` don't affect the Ingress after it is created.

sources.title: About GKE Ingress routing and security
sources.evidence: Use a `BackendConfig` CRD to have the most control over the load balancer health check settings.

stem: You expose an app with a GKE Gateway. Every path of the app, including `/` and `/healthz`, returns HTTP 401 without an `Authorization` header. The readiness probe on `/healthz` sends this header, so the Pods are ready. The load balancer marks all backends unhealthy. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add an `Authorization` header to the health check in a HealthCheckPolicy.
Create a BackendConfig with a `healthCheck` section, and annotate the Service.
Create a HealthCheckPolicy for the Service with `requestPath: /healthz`.
Remove the header from the readiness probe, so that GKE copies the probe to the health check.
Change the app so that `/healthz` returns HTTP 200 without authentication.

explanation: **GKE Gateway does not infer health check settings** from probes, so you set the path in a **HealthCheckPolicy**. The health check needs **HTTP 200**, and it **cannot send custom headers** such as `Authorization`. The health check path must allow unauthenticated access.

whyWrong.A: A Gateway HealthCheckPolicy cannot send custom HTTP request headers, such as `Authorization`.
whyWrong.B: BackendConfig is an Ingress configuration resource. It does not work with a Gateway.
whyWrong.D: GKE Gateway does not read readiness or liveness probes. Without the header, the Pods would also fail the readiness probe.

sources.title: Configure Gateway resources using Policies
sources.evidence: Unlike GKE Ingress, GKE Gateway does not automatically infer health check parameters (such as path, port, or protocol) from your Pod's readiness or liveness probes.

sources.title: Configure Gateway resources using Policies
sources.evidence: You cannot configure custom HTTP request headers (such as `Authorization` headers) in GKE Gateway `HealthCheckPolicy` probes.

sources.title: Configure Gateway resources using Policies
sources.evidence: If your backend requires authentication headers, you must configure your application to allow unauthenticated access specifically to your dedicated health check path (for example, `/healthz` or `/ping`) for Google Cloud health check IP ranges.

stem: During each rolling update of a Deployment, some clients get connection errors for a few seconds. The app stops listening as soon as it gets `SIGTERM`. Which two changes reduce these errors? (Choose two.)

options.text: Change the app to keep serving requests for a few seconds after `SIGTERM`.
Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 5`, so that the old Pods stop and leave faster.
Make the liveness probe fail as soon as the app receives `SIGTERM`.
Add a `preStop` hook that sleeps for a few seconds before `SIGTERM`.
Change the Deployment strategy type from `RollingUpdate` to `Recreate`.

explanation: Kubernetes updates kube-proxies and load balancers **asynchronously**, so new requests can still arrive after `SIGTERM`. Google says **not to stop accepting requests right after `SIGTERM`**. If you cannot change the app, a **`preStop` sleep** postpones `SIGTERM`.

whyWrong.B: A shorter grace period kills the Pods sooner. Requests that are still in progress then fail.
whyWrong.C: A liveness failure restarts the container. It does not stop new requests from arriving.
whyWrong.E: `Recreate` stops all Pods before it creates new ones, so all clients get errors during the update.

sources.title: Best practices for running cost-optimized Kubernetes applications on GKE
sources.evidence: Don't stop accepting new requests right after `SIGTERM`. Your application must not stop immediately, but instead finish all requests that are in flight and still listen to incoming connections that arrive after the Pod termination begins.

sources.title: Best practices for running cost-optimized Kubernetes applications on GKE
sources.evidence: One common strategy is to execute, in the `preStop` hook, a sleep of a few seconds to postpone the `SIGTERM`.

sources.title: Best practices for running cost-optimized Kubernetes applications on GKE
sources.evidence: It might take a while for Kubernetes to update all kube-proxies and load balancers.

stem: A Pod has a `preStop` hook that sleeps for 20 seconds. After the hook, the app needs about 25 seconds to drain its connections. The Pod uses the default grace period of 30 seconds. The app often gets `SIGKILL` before it finishes. What should you do?

options.text: Move the sleep from the `preStop` hook to a `postStart` hook in the same container.
Set a probe-level `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` of 60 seconds on the readiness probe.
Increase `progressDeadlineSeconds` on the Deployment, so that the shutdown has more time.
Increase `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` in the Pod spec to cover the hook and the drain.

explanation: The **grace period covers the `preStop` hook and the normal stop together**. Here they need about 45 seconds, but the grace period is 30 seconds. Increase `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to suit the app.

whyWrong.A: A `postStart` hook runs when the container is created. It does not delay the shutdown.
whyWrong.B: Probe-level `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` cannot be set for readiness probes.
whyWrong.C: `progressDeadlineSeconds` sets how long a rollout can go without progress. It does not change the shutdown time.

sources.title: Container Lifecycle Hooks | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: This grace period applies to the total time it takes for both the `PreStop` hook to execute and for the Container to stop normally.

sources.title: Pod Lifecycle | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: If the `preStop` hook needs longer to complete than the default grace period allows, you must modify `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to suit this.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: Probe-level `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` cannot be set for readiness probes.

stem: A Deployment is behind a GKE Ingress with container-native load balancing. The new version serves its health endpoint at `/healthz`, and `/` now returns HTTP 404. The load balancer health check still uses `/`. After `kubectl apply`, the rollout stops after one new Pod. `kubectl get pods -o wide` shows `0/1` in the `READINESS GATES` column for that Pod. What should you do?

options.text: Increase `progressDeadlineSeconds`, so that the rollout has more time to complete.
Set `maxSurge: 100%` on the Deployment, so that all new Pods start at once.
Fix the load balancer health check, for example with a BackendConfig that uses `/healthz`.
Remove the readiness probe from the Pod spec, so that the new Pod becomes ready.

explanation: Container-native load balancing adds a **readiness gate**. A new Pod passes it only when it **passes the load balancer health check**. With a wrong health check, the rollout **stalls after one new Pod**, so fix the health check path.

whyWrong.A: More time does not help. The Pod never passes the health check, so its readiness gate never becomes true.
whyWrong.B: The new Pods still fail the readiness gate, so GKE still does not remove the old Pods.
whyWrong.D: The kubelet uses the readiness gate and the readiness probe together. Without the probe, the gate still stays false.

sources.title: About GKE Ingress routing and security
sources.evidence: If such a failure occurs while rolling out an updated Deployment, the rollout stalls after attempting to create one new Pod because that Pod's readiness gate is never True.

sources.title: About GKE Ingress routing and security
sources.evidence: A newly created Pod must at least pass its readiness gate before GKE removes an old Pod.

sources.title: About GKE Ingress routing and security
sources.evidence: The kubelet running on each node then computes the Pod's effective readiness, considering both the value of this readiness gate and, if defined, the Pod's readiness probe.

stem: A gRPC service on GKE implements the gRPC Health Checking Protocol. Its liveness probe is an `exec` probe that runs a health check binary every 5 seconds. On dense nodes, these probes add CPU load. You want a probe that checks the gRPC health status with less overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Use a `grpc` probe on the port of the service.
Use a `tcpSocket` probe on the port of the service.
Use an `httpGet` probe on the port of the service.
Keep the `exec` probe, and change `periodSeconds` to 30.

explanation: The built-in **`grpc` probe** calls the gRPC health check and succeeds when the status is `SERVING`. An `exec` probe **creates new processes each time it runs**, which adds CPU load on dense nodes.

whyWrong.B: A `tcpSocket` probe checks only that the port accepts a connection. It does not check the gRPC health status.
whyWrong.C: An `httpGet` probe sends an HTTP GET request. It does not call the gRPC health check.
whyWrong.D: The probe still creates new processes each time it runs. A longer period also makes failure detection slower.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: Performs a remote procedure call using gRPC. The target should implement gRPC health checks. The diagnostic is considered successful if the `status` of the response is `SERVING`.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: Unlike the other mechanisms, `exec` probe's implementation involves the creation/forking of multiple processes each time when executed.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: In such scenarios, consider using the alternative probe mechanisms to avoid the overhead.

stem: A worker app on GKE exits with a non-zero code when it hits a fatal error. The app cannot hang. The Pod uses the default restart policy. A teammate wants to add a liveness probe, so that Kubernetes restarts the container after a fatal error. What should you tell the teammate?

options.text: Add the liveness probe, because Kubernetes does not restart a container that exits.
Do not add it, because the kubelet restarts the container under the Pod's `restartPolicy`.
Add a readiness probe instead, because a readiness failure restarts the container.
Add a startup probe instead, because only a startup probe restarts a container that exits.

explanation: If the process **exits on its own when it fails**, you do not necessarily need a liveness probe. The kubelet takes the correct action under the Pod's `restartPolicy`.

whyWrong.A: The kubelet restarts a container that exits, as the `restartPolicy` sets.
whyWrong.C: A readiness failure removes the Pod from the Service endpoints. It does not restart the container.
whyWrong.D: A startup probe checks whether the app has started. The kubelet restarts an exited container without any probe.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: you do not necessarily need a liveness probe; the kubelet will automatically perform the correct action in accordance with the Pod's `restartPolicy`.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: For a failed readiness probe, the kubelet continues running the container that failed checks, and also continues to run more probes

stem: An app on GKE is behind a Gateway. A HealthCheckPolicy sets `requestPath: /healthz`. The app answers `/healthz` with an HTTP 301 redirect to `/healthz/`. The readiness probe on `/healthz` passes, but the load balancer marks all backends unhealthy. What should you do?

options.text: Increase `unhealthyThreshold` in the HealthCheckPolicy, so that the backends stay healthy longer.
Change the readiness probe to a `tcpSocket` probe on the port of the app.
Create a BackendConfig with `requestPath: /healthz/`, and reference it from the Service.
Set `requestPath: /healthz/` in the HealthCheckPolicy, so that the check gets HTTP 200.

explanation: The kubelet accepts **any status from 200 to 399**, so the readiness probe passes with a 301. A Google Cloud health check **strictly requires HTTP 200**, and a redirect marks the backend unhealthy. The health check path must return 200.

whyWrong.A: Every check still gets a 301, so the backends stay unhealthy.
whyWrong.B: GKE Gateway does not read the readiness probe. The load balancer health check still gets a 301.
whyWrong.C: BackendConfig is an Ingress configuration resource. It does not work with a Gateway.

sources.title: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: The diagnostic is considered successful if the response has a status code greater than or equal to 200 and less than 400.

sources.title: Configure Gateway resources using Policies
sources.evidence: Google Cloud health check probes strictly require an HTTP `200` (OK) response code.

sources.title: Configure Gateway resources using Policies
sources.evidence: If your application returns redirects (for example, HTTP `301` or `302`) or client errors (for example, HTTP `401` or `403` on authenticated endpoints) on the probed path, the load balancer will mark the backend unhealthy

stem: A stateless service on GKE Standard runs 6 replicas. During node upgrades, GKE drains nodes, and sometimes 3 replicas stop at the same time. This leaves too little capacity. You want at most 1 replica to be down at a time during node drains. What should you do?

options.text: Set `maxUnavailable: 1` in the `RollingUpdate` strategy of the service's Deployment.
Increase `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` in the Pod spec of the service to 120 seconds.
Increase `minReadySeconds` in the Deployment spec of the service to 120 seconds.
Create a PodDisruptionBudget with `maxUnavailable: 1` for the Pods of the service.

explanation: A **PodDisruptionBudget** limits how many Pods of an app a **voluntary disruption**, such as a node drain, can take down at the same time. GKE node upgrades respect the PDB, so only one Pod is evicted at a time.

whyWrong.A: The Deployment strategy controls rolling updates of the Deployment. It does not limit evictions during a node drain.
whyWrong.B: A longer grace period gives each Pod more time to stop. It does not limit how many Pods stop at the same time.
whyWrong.C: `minReadySeconds` affects how a rollout counts new Pods as available. It does not limit evictions during a node drain.

sources.title: Disruptions | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from voluntary disruptions.

sources.title: Node upgrade strategies
sources.evidence: if you create a PDB with `maxUnavailable=1` for one or more workloads running on the node pool, then only one Pod of those workloads can be evicted at a time, limiting the parallelism of the entire upgrade.

stem: You create an HPA with the `autoscaling/v2` API. It targets 60% average CPU utilization for a Deployment. Under heavy load, the HPA never adds Pods. The containers in the Deployment set no resource requests. What should you do?

options.text: Set CPU requests for each container in the Deployment.
Change the HPA manifest to the `autoscaling/v1` API.
Enable the cluster autoscaler on the node pool.
Lower the target to 30% average CPU utilization.

explanation: A utilization target is a **percentage of the Pod's requests**. If the containers have no CPU requests, the HPA cannot do the calculation and **takes no action** for that metric. **Set CPU requests** for each container.

whyWrong.B: The `v1` API also needs requests for a utilization target. Google no longer recommends the `v1` API.
whyWrong.C: The cluster autoscaler adds nodes for Pods that cannot be scheduled. It does not make the HPA add Pods.
whyWrong.D: Any utilization target needs requests. The HPA takes no action at any target value.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: To use resource utilization percentage targets with horizontal Pod autoscaling, you must configure requests for that resource for each container running in each Pod in the workload.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: Otherwise, the horizontal Pod autoscaler cannot perform the calculations it needs to, and takes no action related to that metric.

stem: An HPA on a GKE Standard cluster raises a Deployment from 4 to 12 replicas during a traffic peak. The node pool has a fixed size. Five new Pods stay `Pending`, because no node has room for their requests. The requests match the real use of the app. What should you do?

options.text: Increase `maxReplicas` in the HPA, so that it can add more Pods.
Enable the cluster autoscaler on the node pool, with a minimum and a maximum size.
Turn on Compute Engine autoscaling for the managed instance group of the node pool.
Lower the CPU requests of the Pods, so that more Pods fit on each node.

explanation: **The HPA does not change the number of nodes.** The **cluster autoscaler** adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled, and it decides from Pod requests.

whyWrong.A: More replicas create more `Pending` Pods. The HPA does not add nodes.
whyWrong.C: Compute Engine autoscaling conflicts with the cluster autoscaler. Google says not to turn it on for cluster nodes.
whyWrong.D: The requests match real use, so smaller requests would overload the nodes. The cluster autoscaler also needs correct requests.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: Horizontal Pod autoscaling doesn't change the number of nodes in a GKE cluster. To automatically scale the number of nodes in the cluster based on changes in the number of Pods, you can use the cluster autoscaler.

sources.title: About GKE cluster autoscaling
sources.evidence: Don't enable Compute Engine autoscaling for managed instance groups for your cluster nodes.

sources.title: About GKE cluster autoscaling
sources.evidence: Cluster autoscaler makes these scaling decisions based on the resource requests (rather than actual resource utilization) of Pods running on that node pool's nodes.

stem: An HPA targets 50% average CPU utilization. The Deployment has 4 replicas, and the current average CPU utilization is 80%. The HPA allows up to 10 replicas, and no `behavior` policy limits the change. How many replicas does the HPA set?
explanation: The HPA uses `desiredReplicas = ceil[currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue]`. Here, ceil(4 × 80 / 50) = **ceil(6.4) = 7**.

whyWrong.A: With 5 replicas, the average utilization stays above the target. The calculation gives 6.4, which rounds up to 7.
whyWrong.B: The HPA rounds 6.4 up, not down.
whyWrong.D: 8 doubles the replica count. The count doubles only when the current value is twice the target.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: From the most basic perspective, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller operates on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric value

sources.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled

stem: An HPA on GKE uses the default `behavior`. After traffic drops, the HPA waits about 5 minutes before it removes Pods. The team wants the HPA to remove Pods about 1 minute after the load drops. The team accepts more frequent changes of the replica count. What should you change?

options.text: Set `behavior.scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds` to 0.
Lower `minReplicas` in the HPA, so that it can remove more Pods.
Set `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` to 60.
Raise the CPU utilization target from 50% to 70%.

explanation: To prevent thrashing, the HPA uses the highest recommendation in a **scale-down stabilization window**. In GKE, `scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` **defaults to 300 seconds**. A lower value makes the HPA **scale down sooner**.

whyWrong.A: This setting controls scale-up, and its default is already 0. Scale-down still uses its own window.
whyWrong.B: `minReplicas` sets the lowest replica count. It does not change how long the HPA waits before it scales down.
whyWrong.D: A higher target changes how many Pods the HPA wants. The HPA still waits for the scale-down window before it removes Pods.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: To prevent thrashing, the horizontal Pod autoscaler chooses the largest recommendation from a specified stabilization window. This behavior is controlled by the `scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` field in the HPA `behavior` specification, which defaults to 300 seconds (five minutes) in GKE.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: scale-up defaults to `0` seconds (`scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0`) for immediate activation

stem: A worker Deployment on GKE pulls messages from a Pub/Sub subscription. For each message, the worker waits on slow calls to other APIs, so its CPU use stays low while the backlog grows. The team must keep message latency low. How should you configure autoscaling?

options.text: Create an HPA with a `Resource` metric for CPU, and set a much lower utilization target.
Use vertical Pod autoscaling in `Auto` mode, so that the worker Pods get larger requests.
Raise the maximum node count of the cluster autoscaler for the worker node pool.
Create an HPA on the `External` metric `num_undelivered_messages`, with an `AverageValue` target.

explanation: An **external metric** for the number of undelivered messages in the subscription can **reduce latency before it becomes a problem**. With an `AverageValue` target, the HPA divides the metric by the number of Pods before it compares the value with the target. CPU does not show this load.

whyWrong.A: CPU use stays low while the backlog grows, so a CPU target does not follow the load.
whyWrong.B: Vertical Pod autoscaling changes Pod requests. It does not add Pods to process the backlog.
whyWrong.C: The cluster autoscaler adds nodes for Pods that cannot be scheduled. Nothing adds worker Pods.

sources.title: Optimize Pod autoscaling based on metrics
sources.evidence: Scale based on an external metric reporting the number of unacknowledged messages remaining in a Pub/Sub subscription. This can effectively reduce latency before it becomes a problem, but might use relatively more resources than autoscaling based on CPU utilization.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: In the `autoscaling/v2` API version, this value can optionally be divided by the number of Pods before the comparison is made.

stem: A Deployment has an HPA on CPU utilization and a vertical Pod autoscaler in `Auto` mode for CPU and memory. The replica count and the requests change all the time and never settle. The team wants horizontal scaling and right-sized requests. The team uses only generally available (GA) features. What should you do?

options.text: Replace both autoscalers with a `MultidimPodAutoscaler` that scales horizontally on CPU and vertically on memory.
Set the vertical Pod autoscaler to `Initial` mode, and keep the HPA on CPU utilization.
Increase the tolerance of the HPA, so that changes in requests do not trigger scaling.
Change the HPA to a custom metric, such as requests per second, and keep vertical Pod autoscaling for CPU and memory.

explanation: Google says **not to use the HPA and vertical Pod autoscaling together on CPU or memory**. You can combine them when the HPA uses **custom or external metrics**. Multidimensional Pod autoscaling is in **Beta**, so the **GA-only** rule excludes it.

whyWrong.A: Multidimensional Pod autoscaling is in Beta. The team uses only GA features.
whyWrong.B: `Initial` mode still sets CPU requests, and the HPA still scales on CPU. Both autoscalers still act on CPU.
whyWrong.C: Both autoscalers still act on CPU. A higher tolerance only ignores small changes.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: Don't use the horizontal Pod autoscaler together with the vertical Pod autoscaler on CPU or memory. You can use the horizontal Pod autoscaler with the vertical Pod autoscaler for other metrics.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: You can configure multidimensional Pod autoscaling (in beta) in order to scale horizontally on CPU and vertically on memory at the same time.

sources.title: Vertical Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: You can also use vertical Pod autoscaling with horizontal Pod autoscaling on custom and external metrics.

stem: A Deployment manifest in Git sets `replicas: 3`. An HPA scales the Deployment between 3 and 20 replicas. Each time the pipeline runs `kubectl apply` during a traffic peak, the Pod count drops to 3. Then the HPA scales it up again. What should you do?

options.text: Set `replicas: 20` in the manifest, so that each `kubectl apply` starts at the maximum.
Remove `spec.replicas` from the Deployment manifest, and let the HPA set the count.
Raise `minReplicas` in the HPA to 10, so that each drop is smaller.
Use `kubectl replace` instead of `kubectl apply` in the pipeline.

explanation: When an HPA manages a Deployment, **remove `spec.replicas` from the manifest**. Otherwise, **each `kubectl apply` sets the Pod count back** to the value in the file.

whyWrong.A: Each `kubectl apply` then sets the count to 20, which wastes resources until the HPA scales down.
whyWrong.C: Each `kubectl apply` still sets the count to 3. A higher minimum also keeps more Pods at quiet times.
whyWrong.D: `kubectl replace` also sets the replica count from the file, so the count still drops to 3.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: When an HPA is enabled, it is recommended that the value of `spec.replicas` of the Deployment and / or StatefulSet be removed from their manifest(s).

sources.title: Deployments | Kubernetes
sources.evidence: If a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (or any similar API for horizontal scaling) is managing scaling for a Deployment, don't set `.spec.replicas`.

stem: A worker Deployment on GKE processes messages from a Pub/Sub subscription. It gets no messages at night. To save cost, the team wants the HPA to scale the Deployment to zero replicas at night and to start Pods again when messages arrive. The cluster version supports HPA scaling to zero. The HPA has only a CPU utilization metric. What should you do?

options.text: Set `minReplicas: 0`, and lower the CPU utilization target to 20%.
Set `minReplicas: 0`, and add a memory `Resource` metric next to CPU.
Set `minReplicas: 0`, and add an `External` metric for the subscription backlog.
Set `minReplicas: 0`, and change the HPA manifest to the `autoscaling/v1` API.

explanation: To scale to and from zero, the HPA needs `minReplicas: 0` and **at least one `External` or `Object` metric**. GKE **cannot collect CPU or memory metrics when a workload has zero Pods**, so `Resource` metrics alone cannot scale the workload to zero or back up. The subscription backlog shows the demand while no Pods run.

whyWrong.A: CPU is a `Resource` metric. With only `Resource` metrics, the HPA cannot scale to zero at any target.
whyWrong.B: Memory is also a `Resource` metric. GKE cannot collect it when the workload has zero Pods.
whyWrong.D: The `autoscaling/v1` API does not support scaling to and from zero, and Google no longer recommends it.

sources.title: Troubleshoot horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: Check metric types: the HPA cannot scale to zero if it uses only CPU or memory (`Resource`) metrics. You must configure at least one `External` or `Object` metric.

sources.title: Scale GKE workloads to and from zero using HPA
sources.evidence: GKE cannot collect CPU or memory (`Resource`) metrics when a workload has zero Pods, so resource metrics alone cannot trigger scaling up from zero.

sources.title: Configuring horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: The `autoscaling/v1` API is still supported, but is no longer recommended, and does not support certain features such as scaling to and from zero using HPA.

stem: An app on GKE is behind a Gateway. Its CPU use does not follow its load, because it waits on other services. Load tests show that each Pod can serve about 50 requests per second. You want the HPA to scale on load balancer traffic, and you do not want to export custom metrics from the app. What should you do?

options.text: Set `maxRatePerEndpoint: 50` in a GCPBackendPolicy, and scale on the `Object` metric `gclb-capacity-fullness`.
Expose the app with a LoadBalancer Service instead, and scale on the request count of that load balancer.
Set the rate in a BackendConfig for the Service, and add a `Pods` metric for requests per second to the HPA.
Keep a `Resource` metric for CPU, and lower its target so that CPU follows the requests more closely.

explanation: **Traffic-based autoscaling** uses traffic data from the load balancer, so the app exports no metrics. You set the capacity of each Pod with `maxRatePerEndpoint` in a **GCPBackendPolicy**. The HPA then scales on the `Object` metric `autoscaling.googleapis.com|gclb-capacity-fullness`.

whyWrong.B: Traffic-based autoscaling is not supported for traffic through Services of type `LoadBalancer`.
whyWrong.C: BackendConfig is an Ingress configuration resource. A `Pods` metric also needs the app to export a custom metric.
whyWrong.D: The CPU use of this app does not follow its load. A lower target does not change that.

sources.title: Configuring horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: It is configured using a `maxRatePerEndpoint` field on a GCPBackendPolicy associated with the Service, which defines the maximum traffic a Service should receive in requests per second, per Pod.

sources.title: Configuring horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: Not supported for traffic using Services of type `LoadBalancer`.

sources.title: Configuring horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: We recommend that you switch to the `autoscaling.googleapis.com|gclb-capacity-fullness` metric name instead.

stem:
You review this HPA manifest. The team wants the HPA to keep working after each rolling update. The team also wants a slower scale-down policy.

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v1
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: ReplicaSet
    name: web-7d9f8c6b5
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 60
```

Which two changes should you make? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep `autoscaling/v1`, and add a `behavior` section with a scale-down policy.
Change `scaleTargetRef` to the `web` Deployment.
Remove the CPU requests from the Pods, so that the HPA scales on actual CPU use.
Create a new HPA for the new ReplicaSet after each rolling update.
Move to `autoscaling/v2`, and add a `behavior` section with a scale-down policy.

explanation: A rolling update replaces the ReplicaSet, so **target the Deployment**, not the ReplicaSet behind it. The `behavior` field sets **separate scale-up and scale-down behaviors**, and it needs the **`v2` API**.

whyWrong.A: The `behavior` field needs the `v2` HorizontalPodAutoscaler API.
whyWrong.C: A utilization target is a percentage of requests. Without requests, the HPA takes no action for that metric.
whyWrong.D: This adds manual work after each update. An HPA on the Deployment keeps working through each rolling update.

sources.title: Horizontal Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: When you perform a rolling update on the Deployment or Replication Controller, it is replaced by a new Replication Controller. Instead configure horizontal Pod autoscaling on the Deployment itself.

stem: A GKE Standard cluster runs two workloads. A public API gets sudden traffic spikes during sales. A Go backend runs for weeks with steady CPU and memory use, but its requests were guesses and are too large. Which two autoscaling choices should you make? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use vertical Pod autoscaling for the public API, so that each Pod gets more CPU during spikes.
Use only the cluster autoscaler for the public API, so that it adds Pods during spikes.
Turn on Compute Engine autoscaling on the node instance groups for the Go backend.
Use the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for the public API, so that it adds Pods during spikes.
Use vertical Pod autoscaling for the Go backend, so that its requests match its real use.

explanation: Google recommends the **HPA for sudden spikes**, because it adds Pods quickly. **Vertical Pod autoscaling works best with long-running workloads** that have steady use, and it right-sizes requests from historical usage.

whyWrong.A: Vertical Pod autoscaling is for steady-state right-sizing. It is not a solution for sudden, short spikes.
whyWrong.B: The cluster autoscaler adds nodes, not Pods. It adds nodes only for Pods that cannot be scheduled.
whyWrong.C: Compute Engine autoscaling conflicts with the cluster autoscaler, and it does not change Pod requests.

sources.title: Vertical Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: For rapid scaling needs in response to sudden resource usage, use the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.

sources.title: Vertical Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: Vertical Pod autoscaling is designed for steady-state rightsizing and is not a solution for sudden, short-lived resource spikes.

sources.title: Vertical Pod autoscaling
sources.evidence: Vertical Pod autoscaling works best with long-running homogenous workloads.
